note: Sow into a moist, firm seedbed. Late sowing lowers yield potential, early sowing raises the risk of aphids and disease.
The seed needs moist soil to germinate, a dry seedbed delay the germination and gives an uneven crop.
Shoots begin to break the surfaceof the soil, a uniform emergence sets up an even canopy for optimal light interception.
The growing point transitions from vegetative growth to reproductive spike development.
The total number of potential spikelets and yield capacity begin to take shape.
Plants develop side shoots to build ear number capacity, important to manage nitrogen early to support tiller survival.
Deman in high water and nutrient uptake increase as rapid stem elongation begins, protect against lodging and early fungal diseases.
The flag leaf is fully out and powers most of the grain filling, critical time to protect it from leaf diseases.
The ear swells within the flag leaf sheath, critical to keep the fag leaf healthy for grain filling.
Ears begin to emerge from the sheath and flowering follows soon, be prepared to protect the ears from Fusarium head blight.
Flowering is extremely sensitive to drought and heat, stress here causes sterile florets and cuts final yield. This is also the main risk window for Fusarium head blight.
Starch and proteins accumulate in the kernels, driving total yield and grain size.
Grains contain milky fluid, it is crucial to maintain steady soil moisture to prevent shrivelled kernels and secure grain weight.
Grains solidify into a starchy dough, dry down begins, and final kernel dry mass is largely locked in.
Kernels reach maturity and dry down as the crop finishes active growth.
Grain moisture drops to harvest levels, signalling that the crop is ready to be combined before wet weather ruins quality.
